text.p: British railways operator Railtrack Plc hit out at critics on Thursday after reporting a 15 percent rise in operating profits in its first year since privatisation, rejecting allegations of profiteering at the expense of investment in the network.

Operating profits rose to 339 million pounds ($553.2 million) for the year to March 31, up from 296 million pounds last time, on turnover up 137 million pounds at 2.437 billion. The final dividend was increased 7.6 percent to 14.8p, making 22.1p for the full year, covered by earnings of 58.4 pence.

Railtrack's share price jumped 21-1/2 pence to 667 after the results, which dealers said were better than expected. Analysts had predicted headline profits to come in at between 298 and 308 million pounds.
"The tangible improvements in service which we promised are being delivered and we continue to pursue our ambition to create the world's best railway," chairman Sir Robert Horton said.

Horton said Railtrack had helped cut passenger train delays across the network by 30 percent in the last year and vowed to work with the train companies to get more passenger and freight traffic back onto the railways and off the roads.

Railtrack also rejected allegations by pressure group Save Our Railways that the company was making too much money for shareholders while allowing the state of the network's track to deteriorate "to a dangerous extent."
Horton said the company was pressing ahead with its plans to spend 15.9 billion pounds over the next 10 years on maintaining, renovating and developing the network.

"In years to come," he said, I believe 1996/97 will be seen as a turning point in the history of the UK railway industry. We are leaving behind decades of under-investment to allow our customers and user groups to shape our future agenda."

Chief executive John Edmonds said the company spent 961 million pounds on new investments last year, up 29 percent on the previous year, and that it was 105 million pounds ahead of programme in its agreed investment plans.
"The idea that we are underinvesting is totally wrong," he told reporters.

Edmonds said poor track would lead to speed restrictions and consequent delays in train services. Instead the improvement in punctuality and reliability last year had been a dramatic 30 percent he said.
"If track were deteriorating in the way that our Save Our Railways friends are suggesting that result could not conceivably be achieved...We could not maintain punctuality."
Railtrack's pretax profits soared to 346 million pounds from the 190 million pounds reported a year ago, due to the hefty debt write-off Railtrack enjoyed before it was sold off in May 1996.
As a result interest charges plunged to 31 million pounds from 117 million pounds a year ago.

Adjusting for the capital restructuring before privatisation, Railtrack said pre-tax profits rose a more modest 27 percent to the 346 million pounds, which includes 38 million pounds from property disposals.
"Our operating profit is up by 15 percent and the vague references in the press to much higher increases are not comparing like with like," chief executive John Edmonds told reporters.

He also rejected the suggestion that the debt reduction which Railtrack had enjoyed should make it liable to the new Labour government's proposed windfall tax on excess profits made by privatised utilities.
"I don't think so," he said. "It was obviously an essential part of the flotation process that we had a realistic debt structure...so I don't think the two things are connected."

Edmonds said it would also be "silly" for Railtrack to pay a windfall tax because the industry was heavily subsidised by the government through the track access charges paid by the passenger train operating companies.
Last year the 25 train operators paid Railtrack 2.12 billion pounds, almost its entire revenue.
"For the Treasury to impose a windfall tax on Railtrack when the Treasury itself funds the industry is a slightly circular and tortuous argument," he said.
"It doesn't make it impossible, it just makes it rather silly."

Finance director Norman Broadhurst said that the company had net debt to equity gearing at year-end of just 16 percent, on net assets of 2.665 billion pounds, but this was set to increase due to the investment programme.
($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
